title: Plant Omega-3 vs Fish Omega-3: ALA, EPA and DHA Explained

seo.title: Plant vs Fish Omega-3: ALA, EPA and DHA
seo.meta_description: Chia, flax and walnuts provide ALA; fatty fish provide EPA and DHA directly. See why these omega-3 fats are useful but not gram-for-gram equivalents.
seo.search_intent: Understand how plant omega-3 differs from fish omega-3, what ALA, EPA and DHA mean, and how common food sources compare.

excerpt: Chia, flax and walnuts are rich in ALA, while salmon, sardines and other fatty fish provide EPA and DHA directly. All three are omega-3 fats, but they are not interchangeable gram for gram because the body converts only a limited amount of ALA into EPA and DHA.
content_html:
A food label or nutrition list can say “omega-3” without telling you which omega-3 it contains. That matters because most plant sources are rich in alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), while fatty fish supply the longer-chain fats EPA and DHA directly. They belong to the same family, but the body handles them differently.

ALA, EPA and DHA are related, not identical

ALA is an essential fatty acid, which means it has to come from food. Chia seeds, flaxseed, walnuts and certain vegetable oils are concentrated sources. EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 fats found mainly in seafood; algae are the original marine source and can also be used to make vegetarian DHA or EPA supplements.

The body can convert ALA to EPA and then to DHA, but that pathway is limited. NIH notes that conversion is generally small, especially for DHA. That is why 5 grams of ALA should not be read as 5 grams of EPA plus DHA.

A serving comparison makes the distinction visible

FoodReference servingMain omega-3Approximate amount
Chia seeds1 oz (28 g)ALA~5.1 g
Walnuts1 oz (28 g)ALA~2.6 g
Whole flaxseed1 tbspALA~2.4 g
Farmed Atlantic salmon, cooked3 oz (85 g)EPA+DHA~1.8 g
Canned sardines, drained3 oz (85 g)EPA+DHA~1.2 g

Chia can contain more total grams of omega-3 than salmon in these servings, yet almost all of the chia omega-3 is ALA. Salmon delivers EPA and DHA already in the forms the body would otherwise have to make from ALA. The larger number therefore does not make the two foods equivalent.

Plant omega-3 is still nutritionally important

The difference does not make ALA a second-rate nutrient. It is essential in its own right. In the United States, the Adequate Intake for ALA is 1.6 g per day for adult men and 1.1 g for adult women. An ounce of walnuts or chia can exceed those amounts.

For someone who does not eat fish, regularly including ALA-rich foods still matters. If a direct source of DHA or EPA is also desired, microalgae-derived products provide those long-chain fats without fish.

“Fish” is too broad when EPA and DHA are the goal

Fatty species and lean species are very different. The NIH food table lists about 1.8 g of EPA+DHA in 3 oz of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon, compared with roughly 0.14 g in 3 oz of cooked Pacific cod. That is a difference of about 1.7 g in the same food weight.

So salmon, sardines, mackerel and herring usually contribute much more long-chain omega-3 than very lean fish. Protein may be similar, but the fatty-acid profile is not.

Serving fish brings another practical question: species choice

Seafood is also a source of protein, vitamin B12, selenium and other nutrients, but species vary in mercury. U.S. guidance encourages adults to eat seafood regularly while choosing a variety of options, with special advice for people who are pregnant, breastfeeding or feeding young children. That safety question is separate from the ALA-versus-EPA/DHA distinction, but it can influence which fish makes sense most often.

The useful way to compare omega-3 sources

If the question is whether a food supplies ALA, look directly at its ALA content. If the goal is EPA and DHA, compare EPA and DHA rather than adding every omega-3 into one total. Plant foods and fish can both make valuable contributions; they simply do not deliver the same omega-3 package.

faq.question: Is the omega-3 in chia the same as the omega-3 in salmon?
faq.answer: No. Chia provides mainly ALA, while salmon provides EPA and DHA directly. The body can convert some ALA, but the conversion is limited.

faq.question: Do walnuts contain a lot of omega-3?
faq.answer: Yes as ALA. One ounce provides roughly 2.6 grams of ALA, but that is not equivalent to 2.6 grams of EPA plus DHA.

faq.question: Can you get DHA without eating fish?
faq.answer: Yes. Microalgae-derived products can provide DHA and, depending on the product, EPA without using fish.
